adversarialChallenges.strongestCounter: (b): Granger's codified code has NO zoning chapter and its Subdivisions chapter DOES state numeric lines (front 25 ft, side >=10 percent width and >=7.5 ft, rear >=30 percent depth). A writer could read that as a city-wide line.
adversarialChallenges.test: the same chapter says the lines apply 'unless the zoning ordinance specifies differently for properties inside the city limits' and closes with 'The zoning ordinance shall control all building lines; and if there should ever be a conflict between this chapter and the zoning ordinance, the zoning ordinance shall control.' A line that yields to the zoning ordinance is not an unqualified city-wide line, so (b) fails on the code's own words. (c) fails separately: the code presumes districts and a Rezoning ordinance was adopted in 2022.
adversarialChallenges.residualRisk: the zoning ordinance itself was not located; if it was repealed and never replaced, the class collapses toward (b). Named in the row.

adversarialChallenges.strongestCounter: the incorporation clause's adoption date is BLANK in the published code ('adopted on _________, 19____'), which is what a codifier leaves when it has no ordinance to cite; the code contains no district list, no district name and no zoning map. A reader could call this a placeholder and set the row unclassified.
adversarialChallenges.test: two independent clauses of the city's own law point the other way: § 4-180 states the Zoning Ordinance 'is hereby incorporated into this Code of Ordinances in its entirety as if fully rewritten herein', and the code's adopting ordinance expressly does NOT repeal 'Any zoning ordinance or ordinance prescribing subdivision regulations'. Ch. 16 also creates a Planning and Zoning Commission. The blank date is recorded in the row rather than resolved; the class rests on the incorporation clauses.
adversarialChallenges.residualRisk: stated in the row as whatWouldChangeIt.

adversarialChallenges.strongestCounter: (c) is an absence claim, and this lane read only the Village's published ordinance PDFs (driveway, subdivision, speed limit, driveway standards). A village can hold an unpublished line-setting instrument.
adversarialChallenges.test: every published land-use instrument was read and none sets a general line; the single 'building line' mention is a plat-content requirement (the line is drawn per plat), which is CP1's explicit toC shape and not its toB shape. The residual risk is completeness, not direction, and it is written into the row as completenessCaveat + whatWouldChangeIt.
adversarialChallenges.residualRisk: highest of the three class-carrying residuals; flagged for the writer.

adversarialChallenges.strongestCounter: the row rests on the city's Zoning PAGE (map + ordinance titles), not on a read of the Zoning Ordinance's district list, so it could be (a)-by-title only.
adversarialChallenges.test: the page is the city's own inventory of its own zoning instruments and includes an official zoning map dated 2022-06-06 plus 'Ord. 000515 Establishing a Limited Industrial & Commercial Services District'. A city that publishes a current zoning map and a district-establishing ordinance is zoned; the missing district list affects the future TABLE, not the class.
adversarialChallenges.residualRisk: district list unwritten; recorded in the row.

adversarialChallenges.strongestCounter: section numbering in the read text runs 92.xxx (subdivision) and 94.xxx (zoning) with an older 'Ord. 110B' reference, so the text could be a stale codification.

Hays County, the namesake, publishes that it has no zoning authority, so the two are not conflatable.

deadEnds: z2codes.franklinlegal.net / z2.franklinlegal.net (Franklin Legal Publishing code browser, the host the state-wide code survey lists for Hallsburg and many small Texas cities): the host now serves the ICC Code Solutions marketing site (icccodesolutions.org WordPress) for every city slug tried, byte-identical, so it publishes no city codes. Any plan that routes a city through Franklin Legal is dead.

library.municode.com/tx/<slug> for these 19 cities: every slug (including a bogus control slug) returns the same 6,095-byte shell and redirects to library.municode.com/tx. Municode's Texas CITY INDEX does contain an entry for Creedmoor, but clicking through redirects to the Texas index, so no Creedmoor code text is served.

codepublishing.com/TX/<City>/ and codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/<City>/latest/overview: HTTP 403 Cloudflare challenge to every non-browser request (all 19 cities). Not a 'no code' result - an UNREAD path, and for mart (1495 parcels) it is the largest tractable gap left.
cityofweir.org direct PDF fetches from /media/: 403 without a browser session, even with a Referer; only the large ordinance PDF came down. Cloudflare again.
golinda.com ordinances page and mountaincitytx.gov sub-page fetches: JS shell / 403 to fetch; the mountaincitytx.gov PDF itself downloaded fine with a Referer once the URL came from a browser read.
lessons: A state-wide 'adopted code list' is a URL-finding aid, not a source, and its URLs rot: the Hallsburg lead pointed at a host that now serves a vendor's brochure.

A code that OMITS a zoning chapter does not establish that a city is unzoned - Granger's zoning ordinance is uncodified and provable only from the code's own cross-references plus the disposition-table Rezoning entry. Conversely, a city name in a code host's index does not establish that the code is served (Creedmoor on Municode).

The city's own web page inventory is the highest-yield path for these small cities: brand-new zoning codes (Mountain City Ch. 156, Creedmoor's Zoning page) were reachable in minutes once the city's own site was read, and were invisible to search summaries.

Wrong-namesake is not a rare trap: 4 of the 19 rows produced a wrong-state or wrong-city top result, and one of them (Webberville MI) has a full Building & Zoning department and its own amLegal code, i.e. every appearance of authority.
